title: Medical University of Vienna, Austria
paragraphs: I was allowed to study abroad for three months at the Medical University of Vienna in Austria. Although I had longed for the exchange program since entering university, I had been away from English for a long time, so I had never dreamed that I would actually go abroad, but I began preparing, stimulated by the seniors who had returned from the exchange program. Although I could hardly be called outstanding in my year, I decided to study abroad out of the thought that this might be the last chance in my life to study overseas and the wish to broaden my horizons by living overseas and interacting with various people, starting with doctors and students.

The clerkships were carried out at AKH (Allgemeines Krankenhaus der Stadt Wien), the university hospital of the Medical University of Vienna. In addition to my preferred department, obstetrics and gynecology, I chose pediatrics and emergency medicine, and rotated through each for four weeks. AKH is a huge hospital with over 2,000 beds, one of the largest in Europe, and I was shocked by its scale when I first saw it.

For the first four weeks, the pediatrics clerkship, I had been told before dispatch that I would be assigned to pediatric cardiology, but when I went on the first day, perhaps because the message had not gone through, I was assigned to pediatric emergency medicine. In pediatric emergency medicine the doctors and nurses were busy, I could not understand the German paper charts at all, and the first day ended with my just standing dazed in the outpatient clinic. I thought about how I could make the clerkship meaningful, and came to the conclusion that, as someone who cannot speak German, I wanted to take time to see patients carefully on the ward. The next day I negotiated with the professor myself and had my assignment changed to neonatology, where there was an opening for a student. In neonatology, conferences were conducted in German, but the professor explained everything to me in English one by one. Because many children were hospitalized for long periods, the ward itself was relaxed, and the doctors took time to explain brain and heart echo and physical examination. These first two weeks made me keenly realize that to learn here and make it my own, initiative and independence are necessary.

For the latter two weeks I did my clerkship in pediatric cardiology. AKH has a pediatric heart center, and patients come not only from Austria but also from Eastern Europe seeking the latest medical care. Many complex cases that I had never even learned about in textbooks gathered there, and every day I studied a new disease. I did the clerkship together with local sixth-year students, whose curriculum has an examination at the level of the Japanese national examination at the end of the fifth year and has them work in the sixth year as the clinical year. They are treated as staff even on the ward, and are entrusted with everything, from blood draws from CV catheters to the first touch of inpatients, and I was overwhelmed by the difference in level. They were also knowledgeable about treatments and surgical methods and had so much knowledge that it was hard to believe they were in the same sixth year, but I cast off my shame and asked students and doctors about everything to deepen my learning. Because there are many patients with congenital heart disease, almost all patients on the ward were infants, but thanks to the doctor's arrangement I was allowed to take charge of a 16-year-old high school student with acute myocarditis. Even at 16, his English was better than mine, and far from my examining him, I was sometimes followed up on by him instead, and I felt keenly my own lack of ability and was overwhelmed by the high standard of English education in Austria.

In the next department, obstetrics and gynecology, I rotated through obstetrics and gynecology for two weeks each. In obstetrics I mainly observed the outpatient clinic and assisted in cesarean sections. The style of the obstetrics clerkship was to decide for myself what I wanted to learn, negotiate every day, and be allowed to do the clerkship, so at first I was very bewildered at everything being left up to me. However, I was able to see several natural deliveries, which had been my goal, and among them I was also allowed to attend the delivery of an immigrant, as if symbolizing the recent situation in Europe. Because the pregnant woman could understand neither English nor German, the husband translated the doctors' and midwives' instructions one by one to her, a scene of childbirth that is rare in Japan. It was a long, difficult delivery, but the sight of the mother holding the safely born child with tears in her eyes let me feel the depth of the love between parent and child, and I was moved to have been present at that scene.

Gynecology was divided into three stations, Oncology, General gynecology and Endocrinology, and I mainly observed operations in oncology. In oncology there were many patients with advanced cancer, and the operations performed jointly with urology, general surgery and plastic surgery were very interesting. There were many rare operations I had never observed before, such as total pelvic exenteration, and the operating room was always crowded with many doctors and students. In an ovarian cancer operation, the professor of oncology performed a liver resection, and I was also surprised at the breadth of what gynecology doctors can do.

For the last four weeks I did my clerkship in the ER. I mainly observed initial care in the walk-in clinic, and the students' work here was mainly ECG and securing intravenous lines. At first it did not go well, and I caused bleeding and made the drip spray, causing great trouble, but the local students and doctors taught me carefully. When there was leeway, I was allowed to observe initial care of seriously ill patients, attend a lecture on respiratory management, and try out how to use the automatic chest compression device. There too the local students and exchange students explained things kindly, and I am truly filled with gratitude to them. The students who were rotating with me came to the hospital at night and on weekends and holidays too, and I felt their high awareness keenly. I was also greatly stimulated by their attitude of trying to be actively involved in the examination, such as asking patients themselves about the presence or absence of symptoms while the doctor was taking the history.

In my time outside the clerkships I spent fulfilling days every day, playing volleyball, volunteering at Ronald McDonald House, which is also done in Japan, and going to see opera and concerts. I also had many wonderful encounters with local students, friends who taught me German, Japanese doctors, my host mother and my roommates. I was able to study abroad in the most comfortable season in Vienna, from spring to summer, and for me, who had never left Nagoya before, everything was fresh every day.

Looking back, although I was able to make a mountain of fun memories in these three months, what I remember first is the loneliness I often felt during the clerkships and the bitter memories of harsh remarks. I was compared with the local students and told "He is working, but you are observing," and I tasted frustration. During my study abroad I was depressed many times by my lack of ability, but each time I was able to overcome it, supported by the people around me. I was also able to break through that loneliness and gain the nerve to actively try new things, which became a confidence for me. I would like to take this opportunity to thank everyone who supported me for giving me such a valuable opportunity to grow: Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 and everyone at the International Collaboration Office, the professors of Nagoya University, the Academic Affairs staff, my seniors and classmates, my family, and the people I met in Vienna. Thank you very much.
